input:
Feedback control is one of the most fundamental concepts in process engineering, and a level loop on a process vessel shows how it works. A feedback loop continuously monitors a process variable, compares the measured value with the desired value, and takes corrective action whenever a difference appears, helping the process to remain stable over time.

The first element of the loop is the sensor, which measures the level of liquid inside the vessel and converts it into a signal for the next element. Many types of sensor can be used for this purpose, and the choice depends on the application, but its function within the loop is the same in every case.

The controller receives the signal from the sensor, compares the measured level with the desired level, and works out the difference between them, a quantity generally referred to as the error. Based on the size of this error, the controller generates an output signal indicating how the process is to be adjusted to restore the level.

The final element is the component that acts on the process. In a level loop it is typically a control valve on the line into the vessel or on the line out of it, and by opening or closing in response to the controller output, the valve alters the flow and hence the level.

Finally, the sign of the feedback deserves attention. The loop is arranged so that its action opposes the deviation it detects: a rise in level brings action that brings the level down, and a fall brings action that brings it up. This is negative feedback, the self-correcting property that makes the loop work.
target:
A level loop holds the level in a process vessel at the value the operation requires, without an operator touching a valve. The loop has four parts: the sensor, the controller, the final element, and the sign of the feedback.

The sensor measures the level in the vessel and turns the measurement into a signal. A float, a pressure tapping at the vessel base, or a guided radar probe can serve; the form of the sensor does not change the structure of the loop. What matters is that the signal reports the level as the level now stands, continuously and without intervention.

The controller receives the sensor signal and compares the measured level with the level the vessel is to hold. The difference between the two is the error, and the controller turns the error into an output signal whose size depends on how far the level stands from the value required.

The final element acts on the process. In a level loop the final element is a control valve on the line into the vessel or on the line out of it, and the valve moves as the controller output changes, altering the flow and with it the level.

The sign of the feedback closes the loop. The action is arranged so that a rise in level produces a change that brings the level back down, and a fall produces a change that brings the level back up: the feedback is negative, and the loop corrects the deviation it detects.
